weakness: The placement was written in world axes: the wrist always pitched about world y and the bottle bottom was offset along world +x, because in the nominal scene the rack's shelf happens to run along x. With the rack turned 90 deg the bottle was laid across the shelf instead of along it and fell off every time.
how_found: Questioned A1 (shelf runs along world x). Fixtures are moved and rotated in real kitchens far more often than their geometry changes, and the pipeline read the rack's pose only for its position, never for its orientation.
why_missed: I derived the target orientation by looking at the nominal geometry once (rack geoms, region frame) and then hard-coded what I saw as world-frame constants; only translations were taken from perception.
fix: Read the rack's region frame first and derive everything from it: the shelf axis (region x, projected horizontal) sets the finger-closing axis of the neck grasp (horizontal, perpendicular to the shelf axis), the wrist-pitch axis and the bottom offset; both bottle directions along the shelf are tried, hand on the robot side first; both gripper yaw signs are tried for the pre-grasp; the gripper never releases unless the release pose was actually reached.
general_rule: Express every target orientation and offset in the frame of the perceived goal object (its axes, not just its position), and never in world axes that only coincide with it in the nominal scene.

weakness: The grasp assumed the bottle stands upright: it went straight down to 'top of the bounding box minus 3 cm' and assumed the in-hand bottle axis equals the gripper approach axis. With the bottle lying on its side the fingers closed along the bottle axis on nothing (or on its side) and the 60 deg wrist pitch that was meant to lay it down made no sense.
how_found: Questioned A2: the pipeline read the bottle's detected orientation only to find the bounding-box top, never to decide how to grasp. Tipped-over bottles are common in real scenes.
why_missed: The nominal scene only ever showed an upright bottle, so I wrote one grasp for one pose class and treated the detected rotation as noise instead of as information that selects the strategy.
fix: Classify the detected bottle axis (upright vs lying). Lying: top grasp across the body at axis height, fingers closing perpendicular to the detected axis, several grasp points along the body and +-15 deg yaw tried when the fingers would hit a neighbour; lift, turn to the placing orientation at a safe height, lay it on the shelf with the approach along the shelf normal. The in-hand bottle axis is measured after lifting and mapped onto the shelf axis. Added a retry loop that re-detects the object after a failed or lost grasp and checks gripper_holding after lifting and before releasing.
general_rule: Use the perceived orientation of the object to choose the grasp and the in-hand-to-goal transform, with one branch per stable pose class the object can be in, instead of assuming the nominal pose class.

weakness: The neck grasp used exactly one finger-closing direction, the one the later placing motion needs (perpendicular to the shelf axis). A tall box standing 4 cm beside the bottle sat in the path of one open finger, the planner refused the descent for both yaw signs, and the pipeline had no other grasp, so it gave up on every seed.
how_found: Questioned A5 (free space around the neck). The grasp yaw was chosen for the convenience of the place step, not checked against the surroundings, and real tables are cluttered.
why_missed: I coupled two decisions that are independent for a bottle held by the neck: how to grasp (constrained by clutter) and how the hand must be oriented at release (constrained by the goal). In the nominal scene the convenient yaw happened to be free.
fix: The neck grasp now tries a list of closing directions (0, 90, +-45, +-135 deg from the preferred one, both wrist signs) and takes the first the planner accepts; once the bottle hangs free in the air the wrist is turned about the vertical to the closing direction the placement needs (rotationally symmetric object about the approach axis), holding is re-checked, and the in-hand offset is measured after the turn.
general_rule: Choose the grasp from what the surroundings allow, using a set of alternatives, and fix up the orientation the goal needs afterwards in free space (re-grasp or in-air rotation), instead of forcing the goal-convenient grasp in clutter.

weakness: With the rack 10 cm closer to the robot the single release pose (bottom 3 cm along the shelf, 60 deg tilt) sat at the edge of the arm's reach: the pre-place pose was reachable but the straight descent had no IK, the joint-space fallback 'descent' swung the held bottle through the scene, and the pipeline then opened the gripper wherever the hand had stopped, dropping the bottle off the rack or leaving it perched.
how_found: Questioned A9 (rack placed where the one fixed hand pose is comfortable). Fixtures are rarely exactly where they were during development, and the pipeline had exactly one release pose with no reachability alternatives.
why_missed: In the nominal scene the chosen pose was comfortably reachable, so I never saw that the goal region allows a whole family of release poses, nor that my fallbacks (joint-space descent, release regardless of where the hand ended) could do harm.
fix: A list of release-pose candidates inside the goal region (bottom offset 6/8/3 cm along the shelf, tilt 60/50 deg), tried in order; only straight-line descents (several pre-place distances), never a joint-space path for the final approach; the gripper is opened only if the hand reached within 2 cm of the planned release pose, otherwise it backs off and tries the next candidate. Also added a settling press: after release the closed fingertips press the lying bottle's body onto the shelf so it seats flat instead of staying perched on an edge.
general_rule: Treat the goal as a region and keep several reachable release poses inside it, and never execute an irreversible action (release, drop) unless the robot verifiably reached the pose that action was planned for.

weakness: Every grasp of an upright bottle came from straight above (the neck grasp, whatever its yaw). With a board 3.5 cm above the bottle top no top-down pre-grasp exists, so all yaw alternatives were refused and the pipeline gave up on every seed.
how_found: Questioned A5 again, now for the vertical: the round-3 fix added alternative yaws but all of them still assumed free space above the object. Objects under shelves and overhangs are common.
why_missed: The round-3 alternatives varied only a parameter of one grasp family; I did not ask what happens when the whole family's approach corridor is blocked.
fix: Added a second grasp family for the upright bottle: a near-horizontal side grasp of the body (several azimuths and small downward pitches), followed by a short lift and a horizontal slide-out with the bottle before lifting it clear; the bottle is then held across its body and placed with the existing lying-bottle placement (in-hand axis measured, mapped onto the shelf axis, approach along the shelf normal).
general_rule: Keep alternatives across grasp families with different approach corridors (from above, from the side), not just parameter variations of one family, and plan the extraction path out of a confined grasp before lifting.
